explanations.explanation: Joseph it is, friend. The Lord GOD says, "Joseph shall receive two portions." (Ezekiel 47:13) Joseph's two sons were Manasseh and Ephraim (Genesis 41:51-52), and when the tribes get listed later, each of those two has a strip of his own (Ezekiel 48:4-5).

I see why Judah jumped out, it's a big name. But Judah gets one portion, the last strip before the set-apart land (Ezekiel 48:7). The name with two portions is Joseph (Ezekiel 47:13), and his sons Manasseh and Ephraim (Genesis 41:51-52) show up in the tribe list later (Ezekiel 48:4-5).
Reuben gets one portion, sitting right next to Judah (Ezekiel 48:6). Nothing wrong with one portion, friend, I'd take it! The name God gives two portions to is Joseph (Ezekiel 47:13).

True! God says it plainly: "You are to divide it equally among them." (Ezekiel 47:14) No tribe gets a bigger slice than the rest. That's the kind of fairness that keeps everybody happy at a cookie table too.

Here's what God actually says: "You are to divide it equally among them." (Ezekiel 47:14) So the answer is True, friend. Equal shares for the tribes. The text leaves no room for a bigger piece for anybody.

explanations.answer: He swore to give it to their forefathers
explanations.explanation: That's the one! God says, "Because I swore with an uplifted hand to give it to your forefathers, this land will fall to you as an inheritance." (Ezekiel 47:14) The reason is a promise God made. I love that, because a promise from Him is the best deed you could ever hold.

explanations.answer: They won it back from their enemies
explanations.explanation: That's a good guess, but it isn't what God says. His reason is that He swore with an uplifted hand to give the land to their forefathers (Ezekiel 47:14). The text points to His promise, not a win on a battlefield.

explanations.answer: They paid for it with silver and gold
explanations.explanation: No receipts needed here, friend! God doesn't mention any payment. He says, "Because I swore with an uplifted hand to give it to your forefathers, this land will fall to you as an inheritance." (Ezekiel 47:14) An inheritance is something that comes to you, not something you buy.

explanations.answer: Foreigners who live among them and have children
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! God says, "You shall allot it as an inheritance for yourselves and for the foreigners who dwell among you and who have children." (Ezekiel 47:22) So the guest list got longer. It includes the foreigners living among them, and I just love that.

explanations.answer: Kings of the nations who make peace with them
explanations.explanation: I can see the thinking, but no kings show up in this verse. God names the foreigners who dwell among Israel and who have children (Ezekiel 47:22). Those are everyday neighbors, people living right there in the land.

explanations.answer: Merchants who come through to trade with them
explanations.explanation: Passing through for business doesn't make the list, friend. The verse speaks of foreigners "…who dwell among you and who have children." (Ezekiel 47:22) Those are people who live there, not people on a quick trip.

Native-born, that's the word! God says, "You are to treat them as native-born Israelites; along with you, they shall be allotted an inheritance among the tribes of Israel." (Ezekiel 47:22) Same treatment, same inheritance. No second-class anything.

Temporary sounds like a short stay, but that's not how God puts it. He says they are to be treated as native-born Israelites, and they shall be allotted an inheritance among the tribes (Ezekiel 47:22). An inheritance is made to last, friend.
Not lesser, friend! God's word is native-born. He says, "You are to treat them as native-born Israelites…" (Ezekiel 47:22) And they get an inheritance right along with everybody else.

It's actually False, friend. God says, "In whatever tribe a foreigner dwells, you are to assign his inheritance there…" (Ezekiel 47:23) So he gets his land in the tribe where he lives. No separate corner is mentioned.

False is right! God says, "In whatever tribe a foreigner dwells, you are to assign his inheritance there…" (Ezekiel 47:23) There's no special foreigner section. He gets his land right in the tribe he lives in, alongside his neighbors.

The sanctuary, yes! God says of the set-apart portion, "In the center will be the sanctuary." (Ezekiel 48:8) Verse 10 says it again: "In the center will be the sanctuary of the LORD." So it sits right in the middle of the portion set apart.

A palace would be fancy, but it's not what God puts in the middle. He says of the set-apart portion, "In the center will be the sanctuary." (Ezekiel 48:8) The prince does get land, but that's out to the sides (Ezekiel 48:21).
A fortress isn't what the text puts at the center, friend. It says, "In the center will be the sanctuary." (Ezekiel 48:8) And verse 10 calls it "…the sanctuary of the LORD."

That's right! God says it is for "…the descendants of Zadok, who kept My charge…" (Ezekiel 48:11) Those are the consecrated priests. God adds that they "…did not go astray as the Levites did when the Israelites went astray."

Eli, the priest at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:9), is a real name from Israel's story, but he isn't who God names here. God says this portion is for the consecrated priests, "…the descendants of Zadok…" (Ezekiel 48:11) Zadok's line is the one that kept His charge.

Korah, who stood up against Moses (Numbers 16:1-3), isn't the name God gives here. Verse 11 says the portion is for the consecrated priests, "…the descendants of Zadok…" (Ezekiel 48:11) Go with Zadok on this one, friend.

True. God says Zadok's descendants "…did not go astray as the Levites did when the Israelites went astray." (Ezekiel 48:11) That's a heavy line, and I think it's a sober one. The text puts it right beside the ones who kept His charge.

The answer is True, friend, and it's a heavy one. God says Zadok's descendants "…did not go astray as the Levites did when the Israelites went astray." (Ezekiel 48:11) So the Levites did go astray when the Israelites did. That's what the text says.

Sell, that's the first blank! God says, "They must not sell or exchange any of it, and they must not transfer this best part of the land…" (Ezekiel 48:14) That means no selling, no swapping and no handing it over.
Holy is the second blank! The verse ends, "…for it is holy to the LORD." (Ezekiel 48:14) That's the reason given. This is the best part of the land, and it belongs to Him.

This verse isn't about farming, friend. It says what they must not do with the land, and the word is sell: "They must not sell or exchange any of it…" (Ezekiel 48:14) The word for the first blank is sell.
Pleasing sounds nice, but it isn't the word God uses. The verse says the land must not be transferred, "…for it is holy to the LORD." (Ezekiel 48:14) Holy is the word that fills that blank.

Divide is the word for the rest of the land, friend, since the tribes' portions get divided. This verse says something different about this portion. It says they must not "…sell or exchange…" or transfer it. (Ezekiel 48:14) Sell is the first blank.

It's actually False, friend. God says, "The workers of the city who cultivate it will come from all the tribes of Israel." (Ezekiel 48:19) That's every tribe, not just Judah. I'd say that's a mighty big work crew.

False is right! The text says, "The workers of the city who cultivate it will come from all the tribes of Israel." (Ezekiel 48:19) Not one tribe, but all of them. That's a lot of different hands on the city's land.

The prince, yes! God says, "The remaining area on both sides of the holy portion and of the property of the city will belong to the prince." (Ezekiel 48:21) His land runs out east and west toward the borders. And the holy portion and sanctuary stay in the middle of it all.
The priests already have their land, friend. It's the holy portion in the middle (Ezekiel 48:10-11). The land running out on both sides of the square belongs to the prince (Ezekiel 48:21).

The workers do get something, but not this land. The produce of the land God marks out for the city is to supply their food (Ezekiel 48:18). The land running out on both sides of the square "…will belong to the prince." (Ezekiel 48:21)

That's it! God says, "…the gates of the city will be named after the tribes of Israel." (Ezekiel 48:31) Twelve gates, three on each side, and every one carries a tribe's name. The north side has "the gate of Reuben, the gate of Judah, and the gate of Levi." That's a whole city with the family name on the door.
Prophets get a lot of credit, and I'm one fan! But the text doesn't name a single gate after a prophet. It says, "…the gates of the city will be named after the tribes of Israel." (Ezekiel 48:31)
No crowns on these gates, friend. God says the gates "…will be named after the tribes of Israel." (Ezekiel 48:31) You'll find tribe names like Reuben, Judah and Levi up on the north side.

That one's False, friend. The east side has "the gate of Joseph, the gate of Benjamin, and the gate of Dan." (Ezekiel 48:32) So the gate carries Joseph's name. Manasseh and Ephraim don't get gates of their own.

False is right! The east side has "the gate of Joseph, the gate of Benjamin, and the gate of Dan." (Ezekiel 48:32) Manasseh and Ephraim, Joseph's sons (Genesis 41:51-52), each get a portion in the land (Ezekiel 48:4-5), but the gate carries their father's name, Joseph.

THE LORD IS THERE! That's the last line of the whole vision: "…from that day on the name of the city will be: THE LORD IS THERE." (Ezekiel 48:35) After all those measurements, gates and borders, that's the name the city gets. I think that's a pretty fine way to end.
That's a real name in the Bible, friend. Abraham, Isaac's father, gave it to a place in Genesis 22:14. But the city in Ezekiel gets a different name: THE LORD IS THERE. (Ezekiel 48:35)
That's a real name in the Bible too. Gideon, a judge of Israel, gave it to an altar he built (Judges 6:24). But the name for this city is THE LORD IS THERE. (Ezekiel 48:35)
